units.name: Summary Writing
units.summary: Reducing a passage to its essentials without distorting it.

topics.name: Summary Writing
topics.summary: Finding main ideas and rewriting them in your own words.

objectives.text: Identify the main ideas in a passage.
Rewrite them concisely in your own words.
Avoid the common faults that lose marks.

keyTerms.definition: A short version keeping only the essential ideas.
Saying the same thing in different words.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Summary tests whether you understood a passage, not whether you can copy it. This lesson covers the method and the four faults that cost the most marks.

sections.heading: The method
sections.body:
STEP 1 — Read the whole passage once, without writing. You cannot judge what matters until you know where it goes.

STEP 2 — Read again, marking main points. Each paragraph usually carries one.

STEP 3 — Separate MAIN IDEAS from SUPPORTING DETAIL. Examples, statistics and repetitions are detail — they illustrate a point rather than being one.

STEP 4 — Write the main points in your own words, in your own sentences.

STEP 5 — Check the word limit and count. Then check you have not changed the author's meaning.

sections.heading: Main idea or detail?
sections.body:
A reliable test: if you removed this sentence, would a main point disappear, or would the passage just be less colourful?

    "Deforestation harms communities. In one district, 200 families
     lost access to firewood within two years."

Main idea: deforestation harms communities.
Detail: the 200 families. It illustrates the harm; it is not a separate point.

In a summary, keep the first and drop the second. Specific numbers and named examples are almost always detail.
sections.example:
A passage reduced.

Original (about 60 words):

    "Many students struggle to study at home in the evening. Some
     have no electric light, so reading becomes impossible after
     dark. Others share a small room with several relatives and
     cannot concentrate. A few must work in the evening to help
     their families. These difficulties mean ability alone does not
     decide results."

Main points:
    1. Students find evening study hard at home
    2. Reasons: no light, no quiet space, evening work
    3. Therefore results do not depend on ability alone

Summary (about 25 words):

    "Evening study at home is difficult for many students, who may
     lack lighting, quiet space or free time. Results therefore
     reflect circumstances as well as ability."

Notice: three reasons compressed into one list, and "ability alone does not decide results" reworded rather than copied.

sections.heading: The four faults
sections.body:
**1. Copying whole sentences.** The commonest and most costly. If a phrase is lifted unchanged, you have not shown understanding. Technical terms with no synonym are the only exception.

**2. Adding your own opinion.** A summary reports what the author said. "I think this is unfair" does not belong, however reasonable.

**3. Keeping examples.** They are the first thing to cut.

**4. Exceeding the word limit.** If a limit is given, it is part of the task. Going over loses marks even when the content is right.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Summarise in no more than 30 words:

    "Rivers provide water for drinking and farming, and fish for
     food. When factories release waste into them, the water can
     become unsafe. Fish die or become dangerous to eat, and
     families who depend on the river lose both a food source and
     an income."

Then check: any copied phrases? Any opinion? Any examples left? Within 30 words?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Read once whole, then again marking main points.
• Keep main ideas; cut examples, statistics and repetition.
• Use your own words — copying shows nothing.
• No opinions; report only what the author said.
• Respect the word limit; it is part of the task.

questions.question: Which is the most serious fault in summary writing?
options: Writing fewer words than the limit
Copying whole sentences from the passage
Putting points in a different order
questions.explanation: Copying shows nothing about whether you understood — that is precisely what a summary tests. Paraphrase in your own words. Being under the limit is fine, and reordering points is acceptable if the meaning is preserved.

questions.question: "Deforestation harms communities. In one district, 200 families lost firewood access." In a summary, what happens to the second sentence?
options: Cut it — it is an example supporting the main point
Keep it and cut the first
Rewrite it as the topic sentence
questions.explanation: The first sentence is the main idea; the second illustrates it. Specific numbers and named examples are almost always supporting detail, and they are the first thing to cut when reducing a passage.
